newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: EBRD says concerned by Slovak-style privatisation. [CORRECTED 17:25 GMT]
newsitem.headline: EBRD says concerned by Slovak-style privatisation. [CORRECTED 17:25 GMT]

text.p: The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development said on Thursday it was concerned about Slovakia's management buyout-led privatisation and its possible effects on further economic reforms.

"Slovak reform was to a large extent very successful but privatisation focused on the management buyout style, which does not necessarily suit every company and this concerns our bank," Jiri Huebner, head of the bank's Czech and Slovak country team, told Reuters.

Privatisation has become one of the hottest issues in Slovakia amid opposition accusations that the government of Prime Minister Vladimir Meciar is selling off firms to its supporters through sales orchestrated by the National Property Fund (NPF), controlled by his HZDS party.

The EBRD, set up to aid the transformation from command economies to free-market systems in Eastern Europe, has itself been affected by the government's tendency to sell large stakes in firms to management -- usually at well below market value.

The EBRD took a 10.5 percent stake in oil refiner Slovnaft in July 1995 (corrects from July 1996), bailing out a large part of the firm's $112 million issue of global depositary receipts (GDRs) which flopped on international markets. The bank effectively paid the 1,000 crown face value per share.

Then in August, the NPF sold a 39 percent stake in Slovnaft with a nominal value of 6.42 billion crowns ($207 million) to a group of managers and employees of the company for one billion crowns, implying a price of 156 crowns per share.
In an interview, Huebner declined to speak about the Slovnaft management's performance but said the EBRD was soon expecting to sell the stake back to the Slovaks.

"To be honest, it complicates our life a bit and such an experience proves to us that it is unambiguously more simple and wiser to participate here more through credits and less through capital participation," Huebner said.
But he said this referred mainly to small and medium-sized private firms that had problems raising capital.

"Large firms should have no problems obtaining funds. The credit market appears to be interested. But I would rather see them getting credits for longer terms," he said, adding some firms with increasing indebtedness should also consider further capital expansion.
"It's better to pay an additional 50 basis points for one year to get a substantially longer term credit and eliminate... a possible liquidity risk," he said.
Huebner said he saw some room for foreign capital in the long-awaited privatisation of the state's major assets.

"The question now is rather what privatisation style will the government decide for the remaining projects of large firms," he said, adding that the EBRD was interested in participating in some privately run infrastructure projects in Slovakia.
Huebner also said negotiations with shipbuilder Slovenske Lodenice on five and eight-year loans totalling 65 million marks were "stuck" since new ownership replaced the management last summer.
